extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, computer scientists, and general readers interested in Ramsey theory, combinatorics, and computer-assisted proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Determine whether the positive integers can be 2-colored so that no Pythagorean triple is monochromatic; and, for computational proofs, produce and verify a rigorous demonstration (here: a computer-assisted SAT proof) establishing the largest finite cutoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valid 2-coloring (no monochromatic Pythagorean triple)
rubrics_metrics.description: A coloring of the positive integers in two colors (red and blue) is valid if no Pythagorean triple a,b,c with a^2 + b^2 = c^2 has all three members the same color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the triple 3,4,5, if 3 and 4 are red then 5 must be blue. Any claimed coloring must be checked against every integer Pythagorean triple to ensure none are monochromatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-cutoff theorem (existence up to 7824, impossibility at 7825)
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct resolution must establish the precise finite boundary: {1, …, 7824} can be partitioned into two parts with no Pythagorean triple contained entirely in one part, while {1, …, 7825} cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The published theorem states exactly this dichotomy; a proof must demonstrate both the constructive partition for 1..7824 and a proof of impossibility for 1..7825.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAT-based computer-assisted proof methodology (cube-and-conquer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem instances were encoded as Boolean satisfiability problems and solved using SAT solvers; specifically the cube-and-conquer approach was used to split and solve the search space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof construction involved logical and algorithmic narrowing to generate SAT instances, then employing SAT solvers to resolve those instances. Any computer-assisted proof should include the encoding method, the splitting strategy (cube phase), and solver details (conquer phase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Search-space reduction / case splitting to tractable instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the naive number of possible colorings is astronomically large (2^7825 ≈ 3.63×10^2355), the approach must logically and algorithmically reduce the search space (the authors narrowed it to around a trillion cases) before applying SAT solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation should explain how the search space was reduced (symmetries, forced assignments, decomposition into cubes, etc.) and provide evidence that the reduced cases are exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof output format, size, and verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer-assisted proof produced a large propositional proof (reported as 200 terabytes) that was compressed (to 68 gigabytes) and must be verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trustworthy result must provide a machine-checkable proof object or sufficient artifacts to allow independent verification; the format, compression, and verification procedure should be documented so others can validate the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational resources and reproducibility notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The reported computation required substantial resources (about 4 CPU-years of computation performed over two days on the Stampede supercomputer at TACC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should report hardware, wall-clock time, parallelization, software versions, and any environment details necessary to reproduce or plausibly re-run the computation or verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive description of a family of valid colorings
rubrics_metrics.description: For the constructive part (existence up to 7824), exhibit or describe a family of colorings for {1,…,7824} with degrees of freedom (e.g., positions that can be colored either color while preserving the condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing explicit examples, patterns, or an OEIS sequence (the article references sequence A383181) helps validate the constructive claim and illustrates the nature of solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and community validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation of the work in an appropriate peer-reviewed venue (here: SAT 2016 proceedings) and recognition (best paper award) is part of validating the approach and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rigorous claim should be accompanied by a full write-up (paper) explaining methods and results, and ideally by community scrutiny, reviews, and independent follow-up work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope for generalizations and open problems (k-colorings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension to more than two colors (k ≥ 3) remains open; any broader claim should address such generalizations or clarify that they are unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors or solvers should state explicitly whether their methods extend to k-colorings or why they do not, and identify remaining open questions and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition / prize attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical/practical significance is indicated by a prize offered by Ronald Graham ($100) for the problem, which was awarded to the solvers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a technical criterion, recording awards or prizes documents external recognition of the solution and can serve as evidence of community acceptance.
